bp: A modern factory is no longer controlled by one stream of evidence. Cameras inspect surfaces, sensors measure temperature or vibration, cyber and operational logs record machine behavior, and workers respond to alarms or dashboards. The paper asks what happens when these different kinds of signals are joined into one manufacturing AI system. The practical concern is safety and accountability on a production line: a system may act correctly when each part is tested alone, yet fail when a camera view, a sensor reading, a control log, and a human interpretation do not line up. This survey serves the people who must deploy and govern those systems, not just train them. It reviews studies, industrial reports, and standards from 2010 to 2025 to organize where risks arise. Its starting point is that manufacturing failures often live at the boundary between signal types, teams, machines, and rules.
wh: The hard part is that manufacturing risk is created by interaction. A pressure sensor can be accurate, a vision model can classify a defect correctly, and an operator can follow the displayed instruction, but the combined pipeline can still make a dangerous choice if one signal is delayed, attached to the wrong physical moment, or interpreted differently by another subsystem. Single-model testing misses this because it asks whether one component behaves well under its own inputs. A factory needs a stronger question: when several streams disagree, which one is trusted, who notices the conflict, what action is taken, and how is responsibility traced afterward? The abstract names sensor-vision conflicts, log-control inconsistencies, and human-in-the-loop misunderstandings as examples. These are not just data problems. They cross data collection, model behavior, software integration, work practice, and governance. That makes the risk hard to classify, measure, and fix with one narrow checklist.
naive: A smart beginner would audit each part separately. They might test the camera model on labeled images, check sensor calibration, review control logs, train operators, and confirm that the company has an AI policy. That seems reasonable because each source of failure has its own owner. It fails because the dangerous event can be produced between those owners. The camera may be right about what it sees but wrong for the time window the controller is using. A log may be complete but not aligned with the sensor event it is meant to explain. A warning may be technically accurate but unclear to the human who must act. Separate audits can certify the pieces while leaving the joins unexamined.
ap: The central move is to treat deployment risk as a layered, connected map rather than a list of isolated hazards. The authors conduct a structured review of more than 80 relevant sources, including peer-reviewed studies, industrial reports, and international standards. From that evidence they build a taxonomy, meaning an organized set of categories, for manufacturing AI systems that combine several signal types. The five layers are data, model, system, organisational, and governance or ethical. The important design choice is that the layers are linked. A delayed sensor reading is not only a data issue; it may make a model output unreliable, create a mismatch with a control action, confuse a human operator, and raise accountability questions. The paper then connects risk categories to mitigation approaches: technical controls, human-centered operating practices, and standards-driven governance mechanisms such as NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 23894, and ISO/IEC 42001.
mech: The mechanism begins with evidence gathering. The inputs are studies, industrial reports, and standards published from 2010 through 2025, filtered into more than 80 sources relevant to manufacturing AI deployment. The survey reads those sources for cases where several kinds of evidence meet: physical sensors, visual inspection streams, cyber or operational logs, and human-machine interaction cues. It then looks for repeated boundary failures. A boundary failure is a place where one stream must be matched with another, such as a sensor measurement with an image, a log entry with a control command, or a model alert with a worker's decision. The paper sorts these failures into five layers. The data layer concerns timing, missingness, mismatch, and interpretation of raw signals. The model layer concerns how learned decision rules handle conflicting or incomplete inputs. The system layer concerns the deployed pipeline, including logs, controls, latency, and integration. The organisational layer concerns roles, procedures, and human response. The governance and ethical layer concerns standards, accountability, and documented responsibility. The output is not a prediction model. It is a risk map that pairs categories of failure with possible mitigations across technical controls, operational practice, and formal governance.
math: This is a survey and taxonomy paper, so its mathematical structure is lighter than a paper that trains a predictor. Still, there is a clear organizing logic. The main idea is classification by shared cause: many observed failures are grouped by where the mismatch enters and how it can propagate. Classification is a mathematical habit before it is a technical label: it draws boundaries around cases so that similar problems can be counted, compared, and handled together. The second idea is systems reasoning, where a factory is treated as connected parts rather than independent boxes. In plain terms, a small error can travel if the next part accepts it as truth. The third idea is risk mapping. Risk combines the unwanted event, the pathway that makes it possible, and the controls that reduce its chance or damage. The paper's five layers act like coordinates for locating a failure. The tradeoff is simplicity versus completeness. A taxonomy must compress messy industrial reality into usable categories, but too much compression can hide the exact timing, authority, or physical condition that made one incident different from another.
dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas, even though it is not mainly a model-building paper. It touches multimodal AI because the central object is a system that joins images, sensor measurements, logs, and human cues. It connects to reliability because the question is not only whether a prediction is accurate, but whether a deployed pipeline behaves safely when evidence conflicts. It connects to privacy and governance-adjacent work because standards and accountability decide what must be recorded, who may inspect it, and how responsibility is assigned after failure. It also neighbors systems papers: latency, logging, control flow, and integration can matter as much as model quality. Compared with recommendation or retrieval papers that rank candidates from many signals, this paper studies the darker version of the same issue: combining signals can improve decisions, but only if the boundaries between them are understood. The theme is manufacturing AI governance because the method turns technical mismatch into auditable organizational responsibility.
ww: The approach works because cross-modal failures become visible only when the review follows the path of evidence through the whole socio-technical pipeline. If a sensor and camera disagree, the important question is not which source is usually more accurate in isolation. The important question is how the deployed system resolves that disagreement at the moment an action is needed. By organizing failures into data, model, system, organisational, and governance layers, the taxonomy gives reviewers several places to look for the same incident. That reduces the chance that a boundary problem is mislabeled as a narrow data defect or a narrow human error. Linking categories to mitigations also matters. A timing mismatch may need a technical synchronization control; an ambiguous alert may need a human-centered operational change; an accountability gap may need standards-based documentation. The structure should improve over a naive checklist because it keeps the connection between failure source, propagation path, and remedy.
po: The payoff is a practical language for inspecting manufacturing AI before and after deployment. The paper gives manufacturers, auditors, and researchers a five-layer map for asking where multimodal risks enter and how they spread across data, models, systems, organizations, and governance. Because the taxonomy is tied to mitigation approaches and named standards, it can support both engineering review and compliance documentation. Its value is not a new accuracy score. It buys clearer diagnosis of boundary failures: delayed signals, conflicting modalities, inconsistent logs and controls, and misunderstandings between people and machines can be discussed as connected risks rather than scattered incidents.
limits: The abstract supports the taxonomy and review scope, but it does not show the detailed source selection rules, coding procedure, or evidence strength for each category. Because the paper is a survey, its claims depend on whether the reviewed studies and industrial reports represent real manufacturing deployments broadly enough. A taxonomy can reveal recurring patterns, but it does not prove that a listed mitigation will prevent a specific accident in a specific factory. The five-layer structure also assumes that risks can be usefully assigned across those layers. Some failures may cut across them so tightly that the category boundaries become hard to apply without expert judgment.
